bull_case: Clinical approvals, trained users, loaned consoles/disposables, NOP logistics density and accumulated transplant operating know-how reinforce each other as volume scales.
bear_case: Open clinical alternatives, powerful hospitals/OPOs, regulatory dependence, supplier concentration and the ability to use NRP/cold approaches keep the moat from becoming an uncontested network monopoly.
thesis: The moat is strengthening from a device/IP moat into an integrated workflow moat. OCS approvals, patents, user certification, disposable pull-through and NOP logistics create switching friction, while revenue and service scale provide operating data and route density. The principal limits are alternative preservation methods, single-source suppliers and the absence of explicit long-term contracts or minimum purchases.

evidence.claim: Heart, lung and liver OCS systems have FDA PMA approvals; patent families extend in parts into the 2030s and 2040s.
Customers are trained/certified on OCS; consoles can be loaned while recurring disposable sets are purchased for each transplant, embedding workflow and consumable pull-through.
Revenue rose from $241.6M in 2023 to $441.5M in 2024 and $605.5M in 2025, while substantially all U.S. customers now participate in NOP.
Q2 2026 service revenue grew 29% YoY and service gross margin improved to 35% from 32%, evidence that logistics density can improve economics.

counterevidence: Loaned consoles do not require minimum OCS product-purchase commitments.
NRP, cold storage/cold perfusion and other warm-perfusion technologies can substitute.
Several OCS components rely on single or sole-source suppliers.
Hospitals and OPOs remain concentrated and sophisticated counterparties.
unknowns: Measured customer switching rates after NOP adoption.
Route-density economics and data advantages versus third-party logistics.
Competitive market share by organ preservation method.
Patent enforceability and practical design-around risk.
falsifiers: If large centers multi-source away from OCS without workflow disruption, switching moat is weaker than assumed.
If service margin fails to improve with route density, network effects are overstated.
Loss of a key patent/approval or supplier disruption would weaken moat trajectory.

hard_veto_flags.rationale: Revenue scale, NOP participation, patents/approvals and service economics show a broadening rather than shrinking moat as of the cutoff.

subscores.rationale: Regulatory approvals, trained workflows, console/disposable architecture and NOP integration create meaningful switching friction.
Multi-year revenue scale, broad U.S. NOP participation and improving service economics provide several primary-source scale/trend signals.
Patents, clinical approvals, consumables and logistics are multiple defenses, but alternative preservation methods and supplier dependencies remain.

uncertainties.rationale: Minimum purchases are generally absent, so switching cost is operational/clinical rather than contractual.
The company does not disclose a standardized network-density or data-advantage KPI.
Alternative perfusion/NRP methods can improve without infringing TransMedics' patents.
